title: Lauren Berlant
keyWorks: Sex, or the Unbearable (with Lee Edelman, 2014)
On the Inconvenience of Other People (2022)
summary: Lauren Berlant (1957–2021) was an American cultural theorist and one of the central voices of affect theory. Berlant studies how people hold on to the dream of "the good life" — a stable job, love, recognition — even when that dream stops sustaining them, and how people live through a crisis that has become everyday.
onEmotions: For Berlant, feelings are above all attachments: we are attached to people, things and scenarios of life, and emotions tell us what is happening to those attachments. The key concept is "cruel optimism": a situation in which the thing we desire gets in the way of our living well, yet letting go of it is frightening, because our whole world rests on it. Berlant stresses that crisis is more often not an explosion but "crisis ordinariness" — a drawn-out tension that people live in day after day. So emotions here are not private malfunctions but ways of adjusting to a world that often wears people down. Berlant offers no heroic ways out — rather, attention to the small ways of catching your breath, holding on and staying in touch with others.

anxiety.text: Anxiety often arrives when the ground beneath your familiar life seems to have worn thin — and this feeling has its reasons. Lauren Berlant describes our time as an era in which the fantasy of "the good life" is coming apart: a stable job, growing prosperity and reliable relationships are no longer guaranteed. Berlant offers the concept of the "impasse" — a drawn-out stretch of time when the old scenarios have stopped working and new ones have not yet appeared, and a person lives in heightened alertness, constantly scanning the world for clues. From this angle, your anxiety is not an irrational glitch but the way your body adjusts to instability. Knowing this doesn't cancel the anxiety, but it takes the accusation out of it: you are not "worrying too much" — you are feeling a real precariousness that very many people share.
anxiety.practice: Write down which familiar scenario — of work, relationships, the future — feels shaky to you right now. Just name it, without trying to solve anything.

fear.text: The fear of losing something important can be especially strong when your whole world rests on it. Lauren Berlant explains why: we are attached not simply to people, work or dreams, but to what they promise — to the sense that life has meaning and a continuation. That is why, for Berlant, it is sometimes frightening to let go even of what harms us: it seems that along with it, our very capacity to hope for anything will collapse. This is the logic of "cruel optimism." Seeing your fear this way means showing yourself some understanding: your fear is not foolish or "too much" — you are protecting a support, however shaky. Then you can slowly, without sudden moves, look for other supports too, so that fear isn't holding up the whole structure alone.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what do I feel would collapse along with the thing I'm afraid to lose? Is there one more support, even a small one?

sadness.text: Sadness can be quiet and everyday, without any particular drama — and that makes it no less real. Lauren Berlant offers the concept of "crisis ordinariness": hardship often comes not as a catastrophe but as a background pressure stretched out over time, which people live in day after day. This kind of sadness doesn't resemble loud grief — it is more like weather. In The Female Complaint, Berlant explores how people share such feelings in an "intimate public" — a community where strangers recognize themselves in one another's stories and feel: "I am understood." From this angle, your sadness is part of a shared experience, not a personal failure. It can be shared: sometimes it is enough to find a text, a song or a person that speaks of the same thing.
sadness.practice: Think of a book, song or film where someone felt a similar sadness. What exactly in it resonates with you?

grief.text: Grief is an enormous feeling, and it needs space and time. Berlant shows that attachment is always more than a bond with a single person or thing: along with them, we are attached to a whole world of expectations, habits and future plans. That is why loss destroys not only the present but also the future that was bound up with it — and that is exactly what makes grief so disorienting. Berlant calls such stretches "impasses": times when the old order of life no longer works and a new one has not yet taken shape, and a person is simply learning to hold on. From this angle, it is normal not to know how to go on living — this is not a failure but an honest state after your world has cracked. An impasse doesn't call for heroism; small, repeated actions that help you get through the day are enough.
grief.practice: Name one small habit that is helping you get through the day right now. You can simply note that you have it.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and that pain deserves to be taken seriously. In the late book On the Inconvenience of Other People, Berlant writes something sober: other people are always a little inconvenient — they change us, get in our way, fail to match our expectations, and we are just as inconvenient for them. Closeness, for Berlant, is never smooth. Sometimes loneliness is fed by a fantasy of connection where everything will be easy and frictionless — and against it, real, "inconvenient" people seem not enough. From this angle, you can gently look at your expectations: you don't have to wait for perfect closeness to feel a little less alone. Berlant also writes about "intimate publics" — about how you can feel a sense of belonging even with strangers who share a similar experience.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person with whom your connection is imperfect but alive. What makes this "inconvenient" connection valuable to you all the same?

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate response, especially when the world demands more of you than it gives back. Lauren Berlant writes a great deal about how people wear out under conditions that promised them "the good life" but did not keep the promise: you work more, yet have less stability. From this angle, one could say that anger often arises where optimism has been disappointed: you invested in something — work, relationships, the rules of the game — and the deal turned out to be one-sided. Berlant calls neither for suppressing such feelings nor for immediately turning them into a fight; rather, for understanding what exactly you were attached to and what did not come true. Then anger becomes not just an outburst but knowledge: it shows you where your trust was not returned.
anger.practice: Finish the sentence: "I'm angry because I hoped that…" — and see what hope stands behind your anger.

shame.text: Shame at "not coping" is familiar to a great many people. In the essay "Slow Death" — which is about the gradual wearing-out of people under hard everyday conditions, not about death in the literal sense — Berlant criticizes the familiar idea that each person is fully the master of their own will and responsible for everything that happens to them. Berlant shows that when structural difficulties — a shortage of time, money, energy — are explained by the "weak will" of individuals, a shame is born that is actually addressed to the wrong place. Elsewhere, Berlant speaks of "nonsovereignty": none of us fully governs ourselves, and this is not a defect but a shared human condition. Your shame can be lightened a little: part of what you have piled onto yourself belongs not to you but to circumstances.
shame.practice: Divide a page into two columns: "what depended on me" and "what depended on circumstances." What part of your shame can you move into the second column?

guilt.text: Guilt can be an honest response to having hurt someone — and then it helps you make amends. But often we feel a different kind of guilt: for not being productive enough, good enough, for "not keeping up" with the life we are supposedly meant to keep up with. Lauren Berlant describes how the modern world places on the individual the responsibility for what is shaped by many causes, and expects everyone to constantly "manage themselves." From this angle, one could say that many of our everyday actions are not heroic deeds but simply ways of getting by, and measuring them against an ideal life is unfair. This helps you tell apart where guilt speaks of a concrete act that can be made right, and where it speaks of an impossible ideal that nobody lives up to.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: is my guilt about a concrete act, or about not living up to an ideal? If it's about an act, what one step is possible now?

envy.text: Envy often flares up when someone seems to be living the very "good life" that keeps slipping away from you. Lauren Berlant describes this fantasy in detail: a stable job, upward mobility, reliable intimacy, the feeling that you are in your right place. After decades of economic instability, Berlant argues, this picture has become almost unattainable for many, yet it keeps pulling at us. From this angle, your envy is not pettiness but an attachment to a promise that the world hands out generously and rarely keeps. In that moment, the other person becomes a screen on which the promise seems to have come true. It helps to ask: what promise exactly do I see in their life? It may turn out that you need not someone else's life but one specific thing — peace, recognition, support — toward which you can look for your own path.
envy.practice: Write down what you envy, and then, in one word, what promise stands behind it: security, recognition, love, freedom?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be frightening: it seems as if your feelings have vanished altogether. Lauren Berlant draws attention to "flat affect" — states in which emotions are not vividly expressed but seem to go beneath the surface. Berlant suggests not treating this muted quality as an absence of life: it can be a way to wait things out and save strength in a situation that has pressed down for too long. In an "impasse," when the old scenarios no longer work and there are no new ones, a person often seems to freeze — and this is a form of adaptation, not a breakdown. From this angle, your emptiness may be a pause you have taken in order to endure. It doesn't need to be urgently filled with meaning. You can simply acknowledge: this is how it is right now, and this, too, is a way of living through a hard time.
emptiness.practice: Imagine that your emptiness is not an absence but an energy-saving mode. What might it be protecting you from right now?

confusion.text: Confusion is a normal response to a world that has stopped making sense. Lauren Berlant describes such periods as an "impasse" — a stretched-out time when the world feels at once very insistent and enigmatic, and the familiar "genres" of life, that is, the ready-made scenarios of how things are supposed to go, no longer fit. In an impasse people don't find a solution straight away: they feel their way forward, improvise, try things, step back. Berlant sees this not as failure but as the ordinary way people adjust to change. From this angle, you don't need to understand right away what is happening and where to go. Confusion is a state of searching, and work is already happening within it: you are noticing that the old no longer works, and that is the first condition for something new.
confusion.practice: Which ready-made scenario — "how everything should be" — has stopped fitting your life? Describe it in one sentence.

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are not a personal failure but often the natural result of a long strain. Lauren Berlant uses the phrase "slow death," and it is important to understand it correctly: it is not about death literally, but about the gradual wearing-out of people under conditions where everyday life in itself demands too much energy. This wearing-out, for Berlant, is part of "crisis ordinariness": it doesn't look like a catastrophe, so it is easy to miss. Berlant also writes about "lateral agency" — small actions such as eating, resting or distracting yourself, which don't solve the problem but give you a breather, a chance to stop being a "function" for a while. From this angle, your pauses are not weakness but a legitimate way of sustaining yourself.
fatigue.practice: What small action gives you at least a few minutes' breather? Allow yourself one such action today — without guilt.

boredom.text: Boredom seems trivial, but it can be oppressive and draining. Berlant writes a lot about "the ordinary" — the everyday in which most of life takes place. For Berlant, the ordinary is not a grey background but a place where unnoticed work is always going on: we adapt, adjust, keep our balance. From this angle, one could say that boredom sometimes arises when life is stuck in an "impasse": the old goals have lost their taste, new ones have not yet appeared, and time seems to have stopped. This doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Boredom can be a sign that a former attachment has loosened and is making room for something else. Listening to it means noticing what you are no longer attached to and what you might be looking for.
boredom.practice: Ask yourself: what used to absorb me and now doesn't? What might that say about what is changing in me?

joy.text: Joy has every right to exist, even when there is a lot that is hard around you. Lauren Berlant writes a great deal about difficult things, but by no means denies joy. Optimism, for Berlant, is the very force that attaches us to the world and lets us move on; it becomes cruel only when the object of desire gets in the way of our living. And joy often arises exactly where a connection truly sustains us: in a conversation, in a shared joke, in a moment when you are briefly free of pressure. Berlant is also interested in the comic — in how laughter helps us bear the awkwardness and mismatches of life. From this angle, joy is neither naivety nor denial of the crisis, but a sign of a living, nourishing attachment. You can accept it as evidence: this is something that truly sustains me.
joy.practice: What brought you at least a brief joy today? Note to yourself: this is a connection that sustains me.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the strongest attachments, and in them we are especially open. In Desire/Love and Cruel Optimism, Berlant shows that when we love someone, we love not only the person but also what the bond promises: a sense of home, of making sense, of a future. That is why love means so much — and why it can be anxious: a whole world rests on it. Berlant also stresses that love is always bound up with "inconvenience": the other never fully matches our expectations, they change us and knock us out of our habits. This is not a flaw of love but its nature. Accepting your tenderness means accepting this openness too, in which you allow another person to change you a little.
love.practice: What promise does this love hold for you — home, peace, joy, a future? Name it to yourself with warmth.

quote.text: When we talk about an object of desire, we are really talking about a cluster of promises we want someone or something to make to us and make possible for us.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a feeling in which we notice that we are being held. Berlant writes almost nothing directly about gratitude, but from Berlant's perspective one could say this. In their later work, Berlant reflects on "infrastructures" — not only roads and networks, but also the relationships, habits and people that make everyday life possible. We usually notice them only when they break down. Gratitude is the moment when such invisible support becomes visible: a friend who answers your messages, a neighbour, your usual morning walk. In a world where so much wears people down, this is important knowledge: you are not holding on by your own strength alone. Gratitude helps you see the web you are woven into, and treat it with more care.
gratitude.practice: Name three "infrastructures" of your life — people, habits or places — that hold you up, even if you rarely think about them.

hope.text: Hope is what helps us live, and Berlant takes it seriously. Optimism, for Berlant, is an attachment to what promises to make life better, and there is nothing wrong with that. But sometimes "cruel optimism" arises: hope is directed at the very thing that holds us back — at relationships that exhaust us, a job that drains us, a self-image we can never reach. Giving up such a hope is frightening, because along with it the ability to hope at all seems to vanish. Berlant doesn't shame anyone for this or demand that they drop everything. Rather, Berlant suggests noticing the difference: which hopes nourish you, and which keep you stuck in place. Hope doesn't need to be killed; it can gradually be shifted toward what truly sustains you.
hope.practice: Look at one of your hopes and ask: does it nourish me — or keep me stuck? You don't need to decide anything, just notice.

quote.text: A relation of cruel optimism exists when something you desire is actually an obstacle to your flourishing.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia can be warm and bitter at once — and that is understandable. Lauren Berlant writes about how, in recent decades, the postwar fantasy of "the good life" has worn thin — a world where work promised stability and the future seemed predictable. From this angle, one could say that nostalgia often longs not so much for a particular time as for the feeling that life has a clear plot and a reliable footing. This is not naivety but an attachment to a sense of security that was — or seemed — possible. Berlant helps you accept nostalgia without turning it into a program: it shows what you need now — stability, belonging. These needs can be respected and given a place in the present, without demanding that the past come back.
nostalgia.practice: What feeling — not event — do you long for when you remember the past? Where in today is there at least a drop of that feeling?

craving.text: A sharp "I want it right now" can sweep over you completely, and there is nothing shameful in that. Lauren Berlant suggests looking at any craving as an attachment, and every attachment, for Berlant, is optimistic: we reach for a thing not for its own sake but for the promise hidden in it — relief, a breather, the sense that things are about to become bearable. In the essay "Slow Death," Berlant speaks of "lateral agency": small acts such as eating that don't solve the problem but offer a short break — something like a small vacation from the will itself in an exhausting world. This idea neither justifies the craving nor shames you for it — it helps you hear what the craving is asking for. If behind "I want" stands "I want things to get easier," you can look for another, gentler kind of break while the wave rises and falls.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, ask yourself: what promise do I hear in this "I want" — calm, warmth, a breather? Write down one word.

quote.text: All attachment is optimistic, if we describe optimism as the force that moves you out of yourself and into the world in order to bring closer the satisfying something that you cannot generate on your own…
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

addiction.text: If your life has long been built around one thing, stepping out of that circle is hard — and it's not a matter of weak character. Berlant's concept of "cruel optimism" describes exactly this situation: what you are attached to gets in the way of your living, yet giving it up is frightening, because your whole familiar world rests on that attachment — the rhythm of the day, the way you cope with tension, sometimes even your circle of people. In "Slow Death," Berlant shows that the wearing-out of people is not a private moral story but part of "crisis ordinariness": when life keeps exhausting people, they hold on to whatever gives them some kind of breather. From this angle, addiction is not a verdict on you as a person but a way of surviving that has become too costly. Such an attachment can be loosened slowly, without bringing the whole world down at once — and better not alone.
addiction.practice: Write down what, besides the habit itself, rests on this circle: a time of day, a feeling, people. If you'd like, you can talk about it with someone who understands — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after can be doubly hard: your body aches, and your head is spinning with anxiety, shame and fragments of last night. Lauren Berlant insists that a person is "nonsovereign": we never fully possess ourselves, and our actions, feelings and bodies keep slipping out of control. Usually we hold on to the image of a "normal" person who is always together — and a hangover painfully shatters that picture. In On the Inconvenience of Other People, Berlant writes that we are inevitably inconvenient to one another; from this angle, one could say that sometimes we are inconvenient to ourselves as well. A moral hangover is an encounter with your own nonsovereignty, not proof that you are a terrible person. You can get through this morning without passing a verdict on yourself: first take care of your body, and put off the conversations about last night until things feel easier.
hangover.practice: Instead of reconstructing last night, do one simple thing for your body right now — and count it as care, not as payback.

euphoria.text: A burst of elation, when everything seems possible, is a real and vivid experience; there's no need to be suspicious of it right away. Berlant writes that we are attached to "scenes" — moments in which the world seems to come together for a while and promises that it could always be like this. Such scenes are optimistic in the most direct sense: they draw us out of ourselves toward the world. Berlant only notes that optimism becomes cruel when we demand that a moment last forever and carry our whole life. From this angle, you can simply live through the euphoria — notice what it opened up, which desires, people and plans suddenly became visible — without turning it into a promise that tomorrow is obliged to keep. Then it stays a gift rather than a debt.
euphoria.practice: Write down one thing this burst made visible to you: a desire, a person, an idea. Let the note wait for later.

crash.text: The comedown after a high — a celebration, a success, a bright evening — can feel like falling into a void, and it deserves gentleness. Berlant describes "crisis ordinariness": life consists less of highs and catastrophes than of a drawn-out everyday in which we somehow hold on. After a high, the return to this everyday feels especially abrupt: the scene where everything promised change has ended, and the world has stayed the same. Berlant calls such stretches an "impasse" — a state in which the old no longer holds and the new has not yet come, and you have to feel your way. From this angle, the comedown is neither a punishment for joy nor proof that the joy was a deception. It is a transition, and in a transition you are allowed to move slowly, leaning on the simplest things: sleep, food, a familiar route.
crash.practice: Choose one very simple support for today — a walk to the shop, a shower, a call — and do it without demanding that you feel better.

panic.text: A wave of panic is genuinely frightening: your heart pounds, your breath falters, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Berlant writes about "nonsovereignty": we never fully govern ourselves — the body, feelings and the world constantly intrude on us. Usually this knowledge is unpleasant, but in a moment of panic it can bring a strange relief: right now you don't need to be fully in control of yourself, and you don't need to defeat the wave. Berlant is interested not in heroic ways out of a crisis but in small ways of holding on within it — whatever helps you live through the next minute. From this angle, you can stop fighting the panic and let it pass, holding on to the simplest supports: the floor under your feet, a long exhale, the objects around you.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Silently name five objects you can see around you.

dread.text: There are moments when the question "what is all this for?" rises up and an abyss seems to open beneath your feet. Such dread can't simply be brushed aside. From Berlant's perspective, one could say it often comes when a big fantasy wears thin — of "the good life," of everything leading somewhere and adding up to a meaningful story. Berlant is in no hurry to replace it with a new big story. Instead there is attention to what holds people up from day to day: to attachments that don't promise the meaning of everything but make life livable — a conversation, a familiar route, someone's hand, a favourite song. Meaning here is not an answer to the abyss once and for all, but a fabric woven together with others. You can let the big question stay open — and still hold on to the small threads.
dread.practice: Write down three small things that gave you at least a little support today — even very simple ones.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are not where you should be is very familiar — and very tiring. Berlant writes about the "intimate public": communities that form around shared fantasies of what a good life should be, and give people the sense that their feelings are shared. From this angle, one could say that a social media feed is an enormous intimate public, where everyone shows their own scene of the "right" life. Your fear of missing out is neither foolish nor weak but an attachment to a promise of the good life that you are constantly shown and rarely given. Berlant reminds us that behind other people's scenes there is also tiredness, doubt and ordinary crisis — it just stays out of the frame. You can notice which promise exactly is luring you — and ask whether you yourself need it.
fomo.practice: Finish the sentence: "It seems to me that somewhere out there, people…" Then ask yourself: is this desire mine — or was it shown to me?

sleepless.text: At three in the morning thoughts seem louder and darker than during the day, and it is a very lonely time. Berlant thinks a great deal about how everyday life wears people down: work, caring for others, uncertainty about tomorrow. In "Slow Death," Berlant shows that this wearing-out is not a personal failure but part of the "crisis ordinariness" that very many people carry. From this angle, night-time thoughts are an echo of the day's tension that found no room during the day. You don't have to believe them: at night everything feels final, but that is a property of the night, not of the truth. Berlant values small ways of resting from the need to be composed all the time. A sleepless night can become just such a time — with no task of solving anything, simply lying there, deciding nothing.
sleepless.practice: If a thought won't let go, write it on a slip of paper and tell yourself: "I'll look at it in the morning." Then notice the weight of the blanket on your body.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds especially deeply, because what collapses is not only a relationship but also the world that rested on it. For Berlant, attachment to a person is an attachment to a "cluster of promises": that you will be seen and cared for, that the future will be shared. When the other breaks these promises, a great deal disappears at once — and even the past suddenly seems unreliable. Berlant stresses that we don't trust out of naivety: without optimism it is impossible to be attached to anything at all. From this angle, your trust was not a mistake but a way of living in the world with others. The pain of betrayal is the price of this openness, but not proof that the openness was in vain. You can grieve the broken promises and be angry without giving up your capacity to trust forever.
betrayal.practice: Write down one promise that has collapsed for you. Next to it — one that still holds in your life.

jealousy.text: Jealousy burns and humiliates at the same time: you want to hold on, and you are ashamed of wanting to. In Desire/Love, Berlant shows that love is not only a feeling for a person but also an attachment to a fantasy of a secure place in the world where you are irreplaceable. Jealousy flares up when this fantasy senses a threat: what is called into question is not only the relationship but the whole structure your life rests on. Berlant also reminds us of "nonsovereignty": in love we never fully control either the other or ourselves. From this angle, jealousy is not an ugliness of character but the anxiety of an attachment that feels its own fragility. You can acknowledge this fragility without trying to defeat it through control, and ask: what am I afraid of losing — the person, or the place they give me in the world?
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: "If I lose this, I will also lose…" Don't argue with what comes out — just read it.

resentment.text: An old grudge is heavy: you carry it for years, and it seems to become part of you. Berlant describes life in an "impasse" — a stretch where the old situation is already over and a new form of life does not yet exist. Resentment often holds us in exactly such a stretch: within it, the bond with the person or event that caused the pain continues, which means it has its own optimism too — the hope that justice will someday be restored. Berlant doesn't call for quickly letting go or forgiving: attachments don't break off on command. From this angle, you can respect what your resentment preserves — the truth about the harm done — while asking yourself how much room in your life you are willing to give it. Easing a grudge is slow work, not a moral feat.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself: what is my resentment still waiting for — an apology, recognition, justice? Just name it.

heartbreak.text: A breakup can feel as if your whole life has collapsed — and that is no exaggeration. For Berlant, love always includes a fantasy of the future: a shared daily life, plans, a particular way of being in the world. When a relationship ends, you lose not only a person but a whole scenario of "the good life" that you were already living in. That is why a broken heart is so disorienting: the familiar cues for how to live an ordinary day have disappeared. Berlant calls such a time an "impasse" — the old genre of life has ended, and a new one has not yet emerged. An impasse doesn't need to be rushed: you can simply stay in it, try small new rhythms, lean on others. From this angle, your pain speaks of how strongly you are able to attach — and that capacity stays with you.
heartbreak.practice: Come up with one tiny new ritual for this week — not as a replacement for the past, just your own.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out any minute is exhausting: every success starts to seem like an accident. Berlant writes a lot about "normativity" — about how we constantly check ourselves against the image of a normal, competent, "proper" person. Such an image is largely a fantasy: real people live by improvising, adapting, learning as they go. From Berlant's perspective, one could say that impostor syndrome is an attachment to a fantasy of complete sovereignty, as if "real" people were fully in command of themselves and their work. But nobody lives like that: we are all nonsovereign and hold on as we go. Your sense that "I'm not quite in my place" is not an exposure but an ordinary truth about being human, which others simply hide better.
impostor.practice: Think of one person you respect and imagine what they might have doubts about. Notice whether this changes how you see yourself.

self_hatred.text: An inner voice that judges you mercilessly causes real pain, and its verdict is by no means necessarily true. Berlant shows that many of our demands on ourselves grow out of the fantasy of "the good life": a successful, composed, loved person who copes with everything. When life doesn't match this picture, we more often blame ourselves than the picture. Yet, for Berlant, in an exhausting world many people fail to cope not because of personal flaws but because the conditions themselves wear people down. The critic passes a verdict on the person but doesn't see the circumstances. From this angle, you can move its voice a little further away and ask: by what measure is it judging, and who came up with that measure? You are more than a mismatch with someone else's picture.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one phrase of your inner critic. Next to it, add: "It doesn't take into account that…" — and name one circumstance of your life.

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything is one of the heaviest feelings, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. Berlant writes in detail about people who live inside "crisis ordinariness," where big decisions are out of reach and circumstances are stronger than any one person. But Berlant notices something else too: even where there is no heroic way out, people find ways to hold on — small gestures of care, habits, conversations, breathers. This is "lateral agency" — the capacity to act not directly against circumstances but sideways, in small things. From this angle, helplessness tells the truth about the limits of your strength, but not that you can do nothing at all. Sometimes the only available action is to live this day a little more gently, and that, too, is an action.
helplessness.practice: Name one very small action that is within your power right now — pouring some tea, opening a window, writing someone a single word.

procrastination.text: "I can't get started" is an agonizing state, especially when everyone around you seems to be working nonstop. From Berlant's perspective, one could say that putting things off is not simply laziness but a form of "lateral," sideways agency: a small step aside from the demand to be productive all the time, a pause from the constant effort of will. In "Slow Death," Berlant describes how exhausted people look for brief breathers from the need to keep holding on. Procrastination is often exactly such a breather — inconvenient, but understandable. Besides, a task can carry cruel optimism within it: too much seems to depend on it, and starting is frightening. If you see in putting things off a request for rest, or a fear, rather than a vice, it becomes easier to take the first tiny step.
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: what does this task promise me if I do it? And what am I afraid of finding out if I start? Write down both answers.

uprooted.text: When you move away or lose your home, what collapses is not only an address but a familiar way of living. Berlant describes the "impasse" — a time when the old scenarios have stopped working and new ones have not yet taken shape, and you have to feel your way, carefully reading every small detail. Emigration and moving are an almost literal impasse: you don't know the local unwritten rules, and the old ones no longer apply. Berlant stresses that living in such a stretch is tiring, and this tiredness is not weakness but the price of constant adjustment. At the same time, new attachments are born in an impasse: small rituals, a favourite café, people with whom you can share your bewilderment. From this angle, roots don't grow back at once — they slowly grow out of such small things.
uprooted.practice: Notice one small thing in the new place that has already become a little bit yours — a route, a sound, the face of a shopkeeper.

overload.text: An endless feed, notifications, news — all of this can bring you to a state where your head is buzzing and nothing sinks in. Berlant describes our time as life in "crisis ordinariness": crises don't come and go but become a constant background that we are forced to keep responding to. Information overload is an almost pure form of this: every piece of news demands a response, and the next arrives before you have had time to feel the previous one. From this angle, your overload is not an inability to "manage your attention properly" but an honest reaction to a world that demands too much. Berlant values small ways of stepping out of constant readiness — if only for a little while, if only in small things. A phone put aside is one such way.
overload.practice: Put your phone face down and look at something still for a minute. Notice that the world didn't collapse during that minute.

unreality.text: Sometimes the world, or you yourself, seems unreal, as if you were looking at everything through glass. It is a strange and frightening experience, and it's important to speak about it gently. Berlant doesn't write about it directly, but from Berlant's perspective one could say this: our sense of reality rests largely on attachments and familiar scenarios — on the day unfolding recognizably and being connected with other people. When life goes on for a long time in a mode of crisis and exhaustion, these threads can wear thin, and the world loses its density. Berlant also writes about "flat affect" — the muted reactions with which people respond to a life that is too strained. From this angle, unreality may be a way of muting too much. Reality comes back gradually, through small touches of the world.
unreality.practice: Take an object with a noticeable texture in your hand and silently describe its weight, temperature and surface.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare feeling that, for a moment, takes you beyond yourself. For Berlant, this is exactly how optimism in the broadest sense works: it is the force that draws us out of ourselves toward the world, toward what we cannot create on our own. Usually Berlant is interested in how this force gets stuck in exhausting attachments. But awe shows its pure side: you reach toward something without demanding anything of it or trying to possess it. From this angle, awe is a reminder that your capacity for attachment is alive, even if everyday life dulls it. It doesn't need to be turned into a plan or an obligation. It is enough to stay near this vastness and notice how, for a moment, the grip of ordinary worries loosens.
awe.practice: Stay another minute near whatever filled you with awe — without taking pictures or doing anything. Just look.

relief.text: Relief is the moment when what was pressing on you finally lets go, and your body exhales by itself. Berlant writes a lot about life under a tension that becomes a familiar background: we hold on for so long that we stop noticing how much energy it takes. Relief makes that effort visible in hindsight — only now is it clear how hard it was. From Berlant's perspective, one could say that relief is one of those precious breathers out of which a livable life in hard times is made. There's no need to devalue it right away with the thought "what if it all starts again." You can allow yourself simply to stay in it, notice your shoulders easing, and acknowledge: you got through it.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and notice where in your body something has let go. Tell yourself: "I got through this."

calm.text: Calm, peacefulness, is a state in which nothing is required, and that is of great value. Berlant describes our life as a constant bracing for crisis: we are always ready for the next blow. That is why calm can feel unfamiliar — even suspicious, as if relaxing were dangerous. At the same time, Berlant pays close attention to the moments when a person steps out of composure, even briefly, and allows themselves a small vacation from the will — not trying, not keeping up appearances, simply being. From this angle, your calm is neither idleness nor naivety but that very breather without which it is impossible to live for long in a tense world. It doesn't need to be explained or earned. It is enough to notice it and let it last.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute without improving anything. If the thought "I really should…" comes up, note it and return to the quiet.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the feeling that a current has opened up inside you and you want to create. For Berlant, this is a pure form of optimism: the force that draws you out into the world, toward what you cannot yet do on your own but can already sense. Berlant is also interested in how such bursts are connected with other people: what inspires is not emptiness but encounters, other voices, books, "scenes" in which a different possibility of living suddenly flashed by. From this angle, inspiration is not only your personal gift but also a trace of your connections with the world. Taking care of it means not demanding an immediate masterpiece from it and not fearing that it will leave. Even if the current dies down, the possibility it opened has already become part of you.
inspiration.practice: Write down where this spark came from: someone's phrase, a place, a book. Keep this note next to your idea.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — a prick of pleasure when something goes wrong for someone else — is a feeling that is hard to admit even to yourself. Lauren Berlant helps you look at it without moralizing. In the essay "Comedy Has Issues" (2017), written together with Sianne Ngai, Berlant reflects on how the comic is connected with the awkwardness and anxiety of living together: we constantly get in each other's way, stumble, look ridiculous. Someone else's fall makes us laugh partly because it releases tension: the awkwardness didn't happen to us. From this angle, one could say that schadenfreude is a similar release, especially in a world where many feel stuck and other people's success weighs on them. This feeling speaks more of your tiredness than of malice. You can notice it — and gently ask yourself what tension it just released.
schadenfreude.practice: Remember the last moment of schadenfreude and write down one word: what tension in you did it ease for a moment — envy, tiredness, the fear of falling behind?

contempt.text: Contempt seems cold, but beneath it there is often tiredness, irritation or fear. Berlant's last book is called On the Inconvenience of Other People (2022). Its central idea: other people are inevitably inconvenient — they don't fit our expectations, get in our way, demand that we adjust. And we can even be inconvenient to ourselves. Berlant doesn't see this as a problem to be eliminated: inconvenience is the very fabric of life together. From this angle, one could say that contempt is an attempt to get rid of inconvenience by placing the other "lower," so that they need not be taken into account. That is understandable: it's easier. But Berlant invites something else — bearing the inconvenience without turning it into a verdict. You can ask yourself: what exactly about this person bothers me so much — and what does that say about me?
contempt.practice: Write: "This person is inconvenient for me because…" — and finish the sentence. Notice how the feeling changes when "they're worthless" turns into "I find them difficult."

disgust.text: Disgust is a sharp "no" that the body says before the mind does: to a person, a situation, sometimes to yourself. In Sex, or the Unbearable, written together with Lee Edelman, Berlant explores how closeness to other people calls our sense of wholeness into question. An encounter with what is other — a body, habits, needs — is sometimes "unbearable": it disrupts the picture in which we are composed and make sense to ourselves. But Berlant doesn't conclude that we must flee from the unbearable: we live with it all the time, and it is also what keeps our bonds alive. From this angle, disgust is a signal that the boundary of your self has been touched. You don't have to be ashamed of it, and you don't have to obey it blindly. You can ask what exactly came too close — and why just now.
disgust.practice: Name what disgusts you and add: "This is too close to…" Don't judge the answer — just see which boundary the feeling is guarding.

revenge.text: The desire for revenge usually comes after a real wound — and in that sense it is honest. Berlant's concept of "cruel optimism" helps you see how it works. Cruel optimism is an attachment to a promise that actually gets in the way of our living well. Revenge promises a great deal: that the pain will go away, that justice will be restored, that you will feel in control again. That is why the fantasy of payback is so appealing — you can replay it for hours. But from Berlant's perspective, such promises rarely come true: the wound remains, and life revolves more and more around the person who hurt you. This is no reproach to your feeling. It tells you where you were hurt and what needs recognition. You can simply ask what revenge really promises — and look for that in other ways, without causing harm: in words, in boundaries, in the support of people close to you.
revenge.practice: Finish the sentence: "If I got my revenge, I would finally feel…" What you wrote is the real need. Where else could it be met?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people closest to you — a partner, parents, children — can be sudden, and afterward comes shame. This is a very common feeling. In the essay "Intimacy," Berlant writes that closeness is always bound up with the hope for a shared story — that the relationship will unfold in a certain way and become a place of rest and understanding. But everyday life with others is also friction, tiredness and endless small demands that don't fit into that story. When reality diverges from the expected plot, irritation builds up. From this angle, your anger is not proof that there is no love but a signal: your expectations and your strength have come apart from what is happening. This is no reason to lash out at others. It is a reason to notice where you are overloaded, and to look for a breather before the anger spills over.
anger_at_loved.practice: Remember the last time you snapped and write down: what "plot" was I expecting from my loved one at that moment — and what was I really missing?

ambivalence.text: Loving and not being able to stand the same person is one of the most tangled feelings, and admitting to it is frightening. Berlant stresses again and again that ambivalence is not a malfunction but the ordinary structure of any attachment. We are attached to people not for a single quality but for a whole cluster of promises: safety, understanding, a shared history. Some of them come true, some hurt. That is why the same face can evoke both tenderness and irritation. Berlant notes that culture offers us simple scenarios — "true love" without doubts — and against them ordinary mixed feelings seem like betrayal. From this angle, your mixed feelings are more honest than many beautiful stories. They don't need to be untangled right away. You can let both be, and see what each of them is protecting.
ambivalence.practice: Write down two promises this person holds for you: one that is coming true and one that hurts. Both can be true.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a gravely ill loved one is often frightening: how can you feel lightness if you love them? Berlant writes about "crisis ordinariness" — a state in which hardship doesn't happen once but drags on day after day: long caregiving for someone ill, an exhausting relationship, constant vigilance. In such a mode a person lives by adjusting and depleting themselves, and often doesn't even notice it. When the tension finally ends, the body lets go, and relief arrives unbidden. From this angle, relief doesn't cancel love: it speaks of how long you held on. Berlant stresses that attachments are always mixed. Love, grief and relief can live side by side, and none of them makes the others any less real.
guilty_relief.practice: Put your hand on your chest and tell yourself: "I held on for a long time. I'm allowed to breathe out — and to go on loving."

indifference.text: Sometimes, where you are "supposed" to feel something, there is silence inside — and that is more frightening than pain. In the essay "Structures of Unfeeling" (2015), Berlant writes about "flat affect" and "underperformed" emotions — about how, in contemporary culture, feelings increasingly show up muted, without the familiar drama. Berlant believes this is not necessarily emptiness: restraint can be a way of bearing too much, a defence of a psyche worn out by constant upheavals. From this angle, your indifference is not proof of heartlessness but, perhaps, an energy-saving mode. A feeling may be present, but in a quiet, unrecognizable form. There's no need to squeeze a "proper" reaction out of yourself. You can simply notice what is happening in your body: sometimes something alive turns up beneath the flat surface.
indifference.practice: Close your eyes for a minute and move your attention through your body: shoulders, belly, throat. Is there even a faint movement anywhere? Just note it, without naming it.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your familiar role — is familiar to many. This is about wanting to change your circumstances, not about leaving life. Berlant's concept of "cruel optimism" precisely describes the situation in which such a wish is born: we hold on to a job, a place or a role because our hopes for "the good life" are bound up with them, even if they have long been wearing us down. Letting go is frightening: the whole familiar world rests on them. The wish to escape is the moment when the body is already saying "I can't go on like this," while the mind is still holding on. But Berlant warns that the dream of escape can itself become a new promise that changes nothing. From this angle, it helps to ask not "where should I run?" but "what exactly do I need a breather from?" — and where you can get it right now, even a little at a time.
escape.practice: Write down: "What exactly do I need a breather from?" — and one tiny form of that breather that is available this week.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to the "wrong" person, or to someone unavailable, often catches you off guard and unsettles you. Berlant passes no moral verdicts on desire — and there won't be any here. In the essay "Intimacy," Berlant writes that intimacy builds worlds: attraction to a person is also a pull toward the world they seem to promise, toward another life, another version of yourself. That is why such feelings can be so strong: what speaks in them is not only a particular person but also what you are missing right now. From this angle, one could say that a "forbidden" attraction is neither a verdict on your life nor an instruction to act, but a reason to listen. What promises are hidden in it — freedom, recognition, aliveness, lightness? That knowledge is valuable in itself, whatever you decide next.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down, in three words, what "world" this attraction promises you. Then ask yourself which of them you especially need right now.

quote.text: Intimacy builds worlds; it creates spaces and usurps places meant for other kinds of relation.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is very common, even though everyone experiences it as if they were the only one. In Cruel Optimism, Berlant describes people who live in an unstable world and constantly improvise: working out on the fly how to behave, what to say, how to look "normal." From the outside it seems that others manage this easily. But for Berlant it is shared work: almost everyone in a group is maintaining a fragile balance and trying not to betray their awkwardness. Berlant also stresses that no one is fully "sovereign" — the complete master of their reactions, face, voice. From this angle, your stiffness is not a special defect but the visible part of something everyone has. Perhaps the person next to you is finding it hard too. This thought doesn't take the anxiety away, but it makes it less lonely.
social_anxiety.practice: Next time you are among people, find one person with your eyes and imagine that they, too, are improvising a little right now. Notice whether anything changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: it's unclear what will happen, and there is nothing to lean on. In the essay "Genre Flailing" (2018), Berlant describes the state of not knowing which "genre" we are living in: is it a drama, a comedy, a crisis, or just a hard period? The familiar scenarios — how people behave in such cases, what to expect — stop working, and we flail about, trying first one and then another. Berlant doesn't consider this a failure: "flailing" is a normal way of coping when the familiar world has been disrupted and a new form has not yet taken shape. From this angle, your bewilderment is not an inability to live but an honest response to unclarity. You don't have to find the right genre straight away. You can allow yourself to try, to make mistakes, and to hold on to small familiar rhythms until the picture clears.
uncertainty.practice: Say out loud what you would title the current period of your life — even a working title. Then write down one familiar ritual that helps you hold on while the genre is unclear.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — drains your strength: time seems to have stopped, yet you have to go on living. Berlant offers the concept of the "situation" for such periods. A situation, for Berlant, is a state of affairs in which, amid ordinary life, something is unfolding that may turn out to matter. It is a state of suspension: we don't yet know how things will turn out, but we are already living in anticipation. Berlant notes that in such periods attention sharpens: we look for signs, reread messages, make guesses. From this angle, your restlessness is not impatience but a natural reaction to suspended time. But Berlant is also interested in how people still live in such intervals: how they find small ways to catch their breath and stay in touch. Waiting can be not only waited out but also, a little, made into a place to live.
waiting.practice: Choose one activity for today that has nothing to do with the waiting — a walk, cooking, a call to a friend — and agree with yourself not to check for news while it lasts.

regret.text: Regret about something done or left undone can keep coming back for years. Berlant helps you see why it holds on so tightly. We live by leaning on the "genres" of life — ideas about how a good life should go: study, work, love, family, in the right order and at the right time. Regret often measures the past with this ruler: "I should have done it differently." But Berlant stresses that no one lives their life as a fully sovereign author: decisions are made with too little knowledge, strength and time, under the pressure of circumstances. From this angle, your regret is not proof that your whole life was a mistake but a trace of what mattered to you. You can ask yourself: do I regret the act itself — or the mismatch with a script that perhaps was never mine?
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and next to it — what you didn't know then and what you were missing. Read it as a description of circumstances, not as an accusation.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a feeling with an exact address. Berlant writes that attachment rests not only on the person themselves but also on what life becomes with them: the rhythm of the days, familiar words, the feeling of being known. When the person is not around, it is not a single thread that breaks but a whole fabric of everyday life. That is why longing can be so physical: you miss not only a face but also the way an ordinary evening sounded with them. Berlant stresses that attachment doesn't end along with presence — it goes on organizing our lives. From this angle, your longing is not weakness but the continuation of a bond that hasn't yet found a new form. There's no need to rush it; you can gently notice what exactly from that life is especially dear to you.
longing.practice: Write down one small everyday detail with this person that you miss the most. Allow yourself simply to stay with it.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — for those suffering from war, violence, injustice — can wash over you every time you open the news. The collection Compassion (2004), edited by Berlant, asks an uncomfortable question: what happens to us when we constantly watch other people's suffering from afar? Berlant notes that compassion can both connect people and leave them in the role of spectators — helpless and exhausted. This is no reproach to the feeling, but a description of its trap. From this angle, your pain is a sign of a living connection with the world, not of excessive sensitivity. But you don't have to carry it alone and without a break. Berlant values small, doable actions: doing something close at hand, talking, caring — and sometimes putting the feed aside to save your strength.
world_pain.practice: Choose one doable act of care for this week — for someone nearby or for a cause that matters to you. And give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: you reached out to a person or a group, and in return — a closed door. Berlant writes that any attachment is essentially optimistic: reaching toward someone means hoping that the world will respond and that there is a place for you somewhere. Rejection strikes precisely at this hope, which is why it feels wider than a single refusal — as if the whole world had said "no." But from Berlant's perspective, one person's refusal doesn't cancel the capacity for attachment itself: it stays with you and can find other addresses. Berlant also stresses that we don't control other people's responses, and nobody gets love by the formula "deserve it — get it." From this angle, rejection is an event in a relationship, not a verdict on your worth. If it hurts, it means you hoped. That is not weakness.
rejection.practice: Write down what you hoped for in this connection. Then ask yourself: where else might this hope find a response — in friendship, in work, in another circle of people?

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned touches the very foundation: it seems that without this person your whole familiar world will collapse. Berlant explains why this happens: attachments hold up not only relationships but also our sense that life has a shape and goes on. The threat of losing the object of attachment feels like a threat to that very shape. In their later work, Berlant speaks of "infrastructure" — of how life rests on many connections, habits, places and people, the way a city rests on roads and pipes. If the whole structure rests on a single support, the fear of losing it is naturally enormous. From this angle, your fear is not "excessive attachment" but an understandable reaction to vulnerability. What can help is not giving up closeness but gently strengthening other supports: friends, activities, rituals.
abandonment.practice: Draw your "infrastructure": you in the centre, and around you the people, places and habits that hold you up. Which one line could you strengthen a little this week?

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts in a particular way: the feeling is real, but there is no answer. In The Female Complaint (2008), Berlant explores the culture of love stories — novels, films, songs — in which people recognize their own heartache again and again. Berlant calls such a space an "intimate public": a community of strangers who feel that their experiences are alike. This is comforting: you are not alone; a great many people have loved and suffered like this. But Berlant also notes the reverse: such stories can keep us in the hope that love will sooner or later redeem everything, if only there is enough of it. From this angle, your pain is legitimate and shared by many. And the question can be put gently: what am I expecting from this love — and are there other places in my life where my tenderness can find a response?
unrequited.practice: Think of a song, book or film where someone loved without being loved back. What helped that character go on living? Write down one thought.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most searing feelings: as if you had been stripped of your dignity in front of others. Berlant writes a lot about "nonsovereignty" — about how no one is the full master of themselves, their life, or how they are seen. Humiliation is experienced as a sudden exposure of this nonsovereignty: you couldn't protect yourself, your image ended up in someone else's hands. But Berlant stresses that nonsovereignty is a shared condition, not a personal disgrace. The fantasy of complete control remains a fantasy, and whoever humiliates is also its captive — trying to assert their power at someone else's expense. From this angle, humiliation speaks of the situation and of the other person's act, not of who you are at heart. What helps you regain your footing is not pretending nothing happened, but being able to tell someone who will listen about what happened.
humiliation.practice: Write down what happened, and at the end add the sentence: "This says something about how the other person acted, not about who I am." If there is someone to tell — tell them.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is very common, and it is not your fault. In the essay "Slow Death," Berlant examines how society talks about bodies and weight: questions of health and lifestyle are turned into a moral story about "willpower" and "proper" behaviour. Berlant shows that such rhetoric shifts onto the individual the responsibility for what is largely shaped by living conditions, work, and access to time and rest. The body becomes a screen onto which social anxiety and shame are projected. From this angle, your dissatisfaction is largely an echo of this moralizing, not the truth about you. Your body doesn't have to be a project for correction. You can try treating it not as an object of evaluation but as what carries you through life every day.
body_shame.practice: When a critical thought about your body comes up, ask yourself: "Whose voice is this?" — and add one sentence about what your body did for you today.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, your familiar confidence collapses, and it is natural to feel angry, afraid and tired. Berlant offers the concept of "lateral agency": not a heroic action that changes everything, but small ways of getting through the day — eating, resting, distracting yourself, spending time with someone. Berlant stresses that such actions are neither weakness nor defeat, but a way of sustaining life where big solutions are out of reach. During illness people are often expected to "fight" and to keep up an unfailingly positive attitude, but there isn't always the strength for that. From this angle, simple steps are valuable too: getting through this day, giving yourself a pause, accepting help. There is no single right way to be ill. There is your way — and it is enough.
illness.practice: Write down one small thing that brought you at least a little relief or pleasure today. That is your "lateral" support.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good feeling, and there's no need to hide it. Berlant writes about a world in which many live at an exhausting pace, and the promise of "the good life" keeps slipping away. Against this background, what you have managed — to learn, to build, to see something through, or simply to get through a hard period — is especially valuable. Berlant draws attention to the fact that sustaining a life in an unstable world is also work, and no small amount of it, though it is rarely recognized. From this angle, one could say that pride is a way of acknowledging your share of that work. Berlant also reminds us that no one acts entirely alone, so healthy pride sits easily alongside gratitude to those who were there. Give this feeling room: it confirms that you are taking part in your own life.
pride.practice: Write down what you are proud of, and add one line: who or what helped you do it. Allow yourself to feel both.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which grief is soft and almost warm. It doesn't need fixing. Berlant writes that we first feel the present and only later make sense of it: the time we live in comes to us as an atmosphere, a mood that has not yet taken shape as a story. Melancholy is exactly such a mood: in it, memory of what has passed, tenderness for what has been lost, and the sense that life goes on all come together. Berlant is interested precisely in such unobvious states that don't fit into the familiar genres — neither tragedy nor celebration. From this angle, bright sadness is not a breakdown but a fine perception of time. You can simply stay in it: notice which images, sounds and memories come with it.
melancholy.practice: Describe your current mood as weather — in a sentence or two, without judgment. What light is in it, what temperature?

quote.text: The present is perceived, first, affectively.
quote.author: Lauren Berlant
